citations.pending: Citations pending review. Information based on traditional use and preliminary research.

A.label: Strong Evidence
A.fullDesc: Strong clinical evidence from multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews.

B.label: Moderate Evidence
B.fullDesc: Moderate evidence from observational studies, case series, or limited RCTs.

C.label: Limited Evidence
C.fullDesc: Preliminary or limited evidence from preclinical studies, small pilot trials, or emerging research. Not confirmed by large RCTs.

D.label: Anecdotal Only
D.fullDesc: Evidence based primarily on historical use and anecdotal reports. Limited scientific validation.

trad.label: Traditional Use
trad.fullDesc: Used traditionally in herbal medicine systems. Scientific evidence may be limited or ongoing.

interactionExplainer.title: What is a herb–drug interaction?
interactionExplainer.whatIs: A herb–drug interaction happens when a plant or supplement changes how a medication works in your body — making it stronger, weaker, or more likely to cause harm. Herbs contain active compounds that can speed up or slow down the enzymes and transporters your body uses to process drugs.
interactionExplainer.ex1Effect: can make birth control, antidepressants, and blood thinners less effective.
interactionExplainer.ex2Effect: can increase bleeding risk with warfarin and other blood thinners (also ginkgo, ginger, and turmeric).
interactionExplainer.ex3Effect: can amplify sedation when taken with anxiety or sleep medications (also valerian).
interactionExplainer.riskLine: The risk is highest for older adults, anyone taking several medications, and people with chronic conditions.
interactionExplainer.actionLine: Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about every herb and supplement you take — and check a combination before you take it.

interactions.title: Known Drug Interactions
interactions.coverageNotice: This list reflects a curated subset of documented interactions and is not exhaustive. The absence of a drug here is not proof that it is safe to combine. Always confirm with a pharmacist or healthcare provider.
interactions.uncitedNote: These pairs are not yet linked to a primary source. Treat them as a prompt to ask a pharmacist, not as a citation.
